utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The solemn declaration to tell the truth which you took at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to the evidence today. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman, had you concluded or are we still with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a procedural matter I would like to take up with the Chamber at the Chamber's convenience, maybe when this witness finishes or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I like to know in advance by indication through the -- either the court deputy or our own legal officer what these issues are so that I can assess whether that's the right way to deal with them. So if at the break you would indicate what it is and that will be relayed to me and we'll decide how best to deal with it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Along that line, Your Honour, if I take it it's something I feel needs to be part of the record that I'll be able to make a record about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. There are ways different ways of doing that in this Tribunal, of course, Mr. Ackerman, so horses for courses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I don't know them all I'm in some kind of trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday when we finished, we were talking about the testimony you gave in the Milosevic trial and we were talking about somethings that you said at page 4039 of that testimony. One thing that you said there with regard to that you were asked if the people that threw the bomb in your house had entered your house and what you said was, "they did not enter the house, they had not come to enter the house but to kill." So it's your position they came there to kill you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't hear the answer but that's because I need to turn this on. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that there were quite a number of them yesterday. I think you said eight or ten right in front of your house and more in the neighbourhood. If they were there to kill you I'm wondering why they didn't accomplish that. Were you heavily armed and shooting back or was your house heavily defended or what kept them from doing what you say they came there to do?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm rather surprised they didn't kill me too. At the moment I was -- at that moment I was not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I guess you have to leave room in your mind then for the possibility that you're wrong, that they didn't come there to kill you or they would have done it, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they certainly didn't come with arms, grenades and Kalashnikovs to have coffee with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suspect that's true but the only thing that kept them from killing you was what they decided in their own minds. You didn't keep them from doing it, did you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You'd have to ask them what was in their minds, if you can find them. I don't know what they were thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that would be nice to ask them what was in their minds but what you're doing is you're telling us what was in their minds. You're telling us they came there to kill you. So you're claiming to know what was in their minds. Now you're saying we have to ask them if we want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he answered the question and said he didn't know what they were thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, that seems to be the position, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's today's position. It was a position in the Milosevic transcript that they came there to kill them and that he somehow knew what was in their minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. Well, I was going to say if you feel it's likely to yield results then carry on but I think you've got as much as to be given from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I could probably ask more questions but I agree it wouldn't be that productive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the area of Drenica. First of all, it's true, is it not, that there was a period of time when the Drenica municipality was under the control of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not in the municipality of Drenica at the time. I only went to Drenica when I had something to do there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Apparently you've forgotten since your testimony in Milosevic. At page 4046 you were asked if all of Drenica was under KLA control for a while and you said for a time it was. So then you must have known that it was. Does that refresh your memory in some way?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the municipality of Drenica. There are actually two municipalities. For the territory of Drenica I do know that for a time it was under the control of the KLA, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know what period of time it was actually controlled by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think from September, October, 1998 until the beginning of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's also the case, isn't it, that the territory of Drenica, as you call it, represents about 27 per cent of the territory of Kosovo, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I've read in geography books.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have no reason to believe the geography books are lying to you, do you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never doubted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During your time in the KLA, from the time you joined up in 1997 until the end, you wore civilian clothes, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And other KLA persons also wore civilian clothes, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them did. Some of them who did not need to wear uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there were women who were part of the KLA too, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were women and girls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they were -- some of them were armed, some of them wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those who were on the front were armed and had uniforms. Whereas the others were busy with other things and they had no need to wear uniforms and did not have arms with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you had four sons who were fighters in the KLA, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about my sons, my children?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, my wife has only given birth to one son.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well then the information I have is wrong, then. I apologise. You know a person by the name of Nusret Pilana [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably mean Nusret Plana [phoen], not Pilana but Plana.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's who I mean. That's correct. My Albanian pronunciation is pretty poor. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with a book that he wrote?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the editor of that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And just tell us generally what that book was about?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which -- exactly which book you're referring to because he wrote several books.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let me give you a title. I think it's called The Terror of Invading Serbia over Albanians, 1844 to 1999. Familiar with that book?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I actually proofread that book together with others, and it's written on the cover of the book who was the proofreading editor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would that be you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I also authorised publication of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you say you authorised publication, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what an editor does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what is the book about, basically?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book talks not in general terms but specifically about Serb occupation and massacres which were carried out from 1844 until 1999, and it's in three languages. The titles, the captions are in three languages. There is a preface which was written and it's illustrated with quite a few photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think that's all I have for you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have questions per se. I just wanted to clarify a few things from the transcript. I was also pretty much convinced that this witness had four sons and, according to the information we've received, that was so. It was in the statement, in the transcript, and all of a sudden I learn he has only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Kabashi, I wanted to ask you something. My name is Toma Fila and I represent Nikola Sainovic. We will attempt to clarify some things, otherwise I have no questions for you. Therefore, you had only one son. Was he a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not trying to make things up. We were advised by the OTP that you actually have four sons. The second question: I can see that you were born in 1941, is that so? Were you born then?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It says here 1941. No further questions. I just wanted to explain. It reads there that you graduated from university and you were probably three years old according to the information provided at the time when you graduated. I just wanted to point that out. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I might, I would like to make a small explanation here. In the press in Belgrade and in Serbian TV, after the bomb was thrown into my house, they wrote that a certain terrorist was killed with my name and then with four children. It was also said a certain terrorist was killed with 11 members of his family. And another version which was on Tanjug was that a certain terrorist was killed with my name, with eight members of his family, all of whom were members of the KLA, like my mother and all the rest. This information was given about me in March of 1999 in the Serbian press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, since you can understand Serbian, we just wanted to make sure that this was not our information. This was OTP information on you. It says that you were born in 1941, the same year I was born, and that you have four sons. It was information provided by the OTP. And I ask myself where is all this taking us? I was about to ask you if we attended the same university at the same time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, you have a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a mystery. We were given a supplemental information sheet by the Office of the Prosecutor which says at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did you receive this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's dated 17 August so we received it around then, and one assumes when you get this it's because they have had additional conversations with the witness and this is new information they've learned from the witness. Now, I don't know now whether the witness told them this or they just got this out of some press release and threw it in here thinking it was him. I don't know. But it might be important to find out. If he told them that it could be pretty crucial, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis, can you resolve this conundrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed that our supplemental information form that did indicate he had four sons was a mistake on our part. I don't know how it happened now but I'm told that was our mistake. As for his date of birth I know the English -- his ICTY statement does have his birth date as 1949 but it appears that the Serbian translation has his birthdate date as 1941. I can't explain how that error occurred but I can understand that's where Mr. Fila had 1941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That seems to clarify the point. Now, Mr. Bakrac, have you questions for the witness? Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kabashi. My name is Djuro Cepic, one of the counsel for General Vladimir Lazarevic, and I will have a few questions for you. Yesterday we discussed the bombing of Pristina and in your statement given to the investigators on the 24th of April 1999, the same thing is mentioned. You re-confirmed what you had stated previously, and that was that the NATO bombing did not cause any damage in residential parts of Pristina and that there were no military installations and facilities in Pristina. You also said that only the prison, the district court building as well as the police building were bombed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the prison, whether it was damaged or not. But the state security building, not the police building, was damaged. They are two different buildings and still are. It was bombed, the building of state security, where investigations were carried out and people were held in custody. If you have photos of the buildings I can show you which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that between the 24th and the 25th of March 1999, during the night, the building of the public housing company, as well as the residential parts of Rudnik and Gavalija [phoen] were bombed?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that, and I don't know where you got the name of Aja [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ajvalija?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Hajvalija [phoen] does exist as an area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise but in the transcript, we don't have the toponym spelled out. It is A-j-v-a-l-i-j-a. Thank you. On the 26th of March 1999, in the village of Gornji Dobrovo, which is the in the territory of the Kosovo Polje municipality, there were six people killed by NATO bombing, four of which were women. All six were civilians.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there at that time. I can't tell you anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in Pristina, the post office and four residential buildings were destroyed and that several people were killed on the 7th of April 1999?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that but I wasn't in Kosova on the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that several residential buildings were destroyed in the neighbourhood of Dardanija, as well as the plastics factory in Pristina and the bus station in Pristina on the 12th and the 13th of April 1999?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read about that, and the neighbourhood of Dardanija and the bus station and the plastics factory are in perfect condition now as they were at the time. None of them were hit, as far as I know. In fact, you can still see writing in Cyrillic on all those buildings as they were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Kabashi. Did you know that during NATO bombings, Pristina and its environs were bombed for 406 times and that over 1.000 projectiles landed on Pristina and its environs?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The numbers you gave I'm not sure about. I don't know. But that military facilities were bombed around Pristina because Pristina was one of the most military cities in all of the Balkans, that is well known, all the military facilities around Pristina were bombed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, I didn't ask you about military facilities. I asked you about civilian buildings and all those I had listed were actually civilian buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying your question about 406 bombing raids and over 1.000 projectiles is confined to civilian buildings?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was a total number of the projectiles in the raids against -- on Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case, the answer was quite proper then. He did not misunderstand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: During your examination yesterday, as well as in -- on page 4, the last paragraph in the English and in the B/C/S, and in the Albanian, this is page 7, paragraph 3, as well as in yesterday's transcript, at page 71, lines 13 and 14, you mentioned that, as you were moving along in that column towards the train station, that a tank was there at the bridge which divided the column. Since this was amidst all the bombing and since you said that military facilities and targets were targeted, how could it be? And I believe you will agree that there was a tank standing in the middle of a bridge amidst all the bombings? Wouldn't it be illogical?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not sure that accurately states the evidence. I don't know that we have evidence that bombing was going on while he was going towards the railroad station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a factual basis for this question, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the time that the witness mentioned is the time during which NATO bombings went on, and I just mentioned a number of times Pristina was bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think we've had evidence about whether the bombs was occurring 24 hours a day every day or only at night or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a question that really isn't for the witness to answer. It's the sort of thing that you might present as an argument, but unless you're going to give him chapter and verse suggesting that there was a bombing raid going on at the same time, then the question doesn't really -- isn't really likely to lead to an answer that will assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we will deal with this question later during these proceedings. Now I would like to deal with something else, if you permit me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, do you know that on the 29th of January 1999, there was a terrorist attack in Pristina in the following way: An explosive device was thrown into a cafe called galleria, eight persons were wounded due to this, and the incident was verified by the OSCE mission? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not in Pristina at the time and I wasn't really interested in who was being killed in the coffee houses in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you're not interested in that? I'm talking about January 1999. Where were you in January 1999, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the January after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No. January 1999, before the bombing, before the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was busy working, doing the jobs that I had to do in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Where were you, then, in January 1999, as a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have been in one of several locations, in Drenica, Malisheva, Dukagjin, or in Lap. I would have -- could have been in Zllashe, near Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And of course, as a member of the KLA, you're not interested in the fact that civilians are getting killed in Pristina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant is I was not paying attention at all to people who were being killed in coffee houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not interested in opinions. Do you know that on the 31st of January 1990, there was yet another terrorist attack?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I apologise. 1999 was what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I said 31st of January 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. A terrorist attack on the Beca cevapcici shop, one person was killed and two were wounded. Are you aware of that perhaps?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the -- that Vienna shop is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So to conclude, Mr. Kabashi, as for all incidents where civilians were the casualties in Pristina are concerned, you know nothing about that, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that's an appropriate question. He's asking him about two and then he says for all incidents, you don't know. Are two the total number of incidents involving civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The point is well made, Mr. Cepic but I wonder in any event where this is leading. Because I'm certainly not going to follow up Mr. Hannis's intervention as an invitation for you to go through all the civilian deaths in Pristina. So really what is the point that you're trying to make? Or what does it relate to, if you can tell me that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. Your Honour, precisely. I don't want to waste the Court's time. I meant -- I thought that in this way, I could deal with this particular set of questions because when all my questions were put about civilians being killed or wounded in Pristina before the bombing, the witness said that he did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've had two incidents referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned incidents during the bombing previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. Cepic, the arguments can wait for later. You've got the answers to the questions you asked and you can build your argument on these answers. Let's move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, are you aware of any incident before the 24th of March 1999 in which civilians were killed due to terrorist attacks in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi -- excuse me, Dr. Kabashi, good day. My name is Dragan Ivetic and together with my colleagues, Mr. Branko Lukic and Mr. Ozren Ogrizovic, I represent Mr. Sreten Lukic, one of the accused in this case. Today I'll have some questions for you relative to your recollection of pertinent for these proceedings, and I would ask that you pay close attention to what I'm asking so we can try and move through this as smoothly as possible. Is that fair enough, sir?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me follow up on the questions that my colleague, Mr. Cepic, was asking about regarding attacks against civilians in Pristina. In the Milosevic proceedings, you testified under oath at page 4019, lines 20 through 25, that in fact no operations were undertaken in Pristina by the KLA in which civilians were killed. Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now the incidents that Mr. Cepic went through regarding attacks on civilians that took place in terms of bombings, that is precisely the type of question that Mr. Milosevic asked you about and which you denied, that those types of operations had taken place, is that not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So it would appear that that portion of your testimony during the Milosevic proceedings was not accurate, isn't that true, Dr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What part of the testimony do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That no such attacks against civilians took place in Pristina. Where we have now heard that in fact there were multiple attacks of which several were identified by my colleague, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do we have evidence of these at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the moment we do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's an argument for you to advance later once we've heard the whole story, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Kabashi, turning first to some technical details, looking at your statement dated the 24th of April 1999, that statement was read back to you in the Albanian language verbatim before you signed it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And after hearing the statement read back to you in the Albanian language you proceeded to sign the statement and certify that the statements that the matters put, set forth therein, were true to the best of your knowledge and recollection; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the Prosecutor has also tendered your testimony from the Milosevic proceedings. Is it accurate to state that you made a solemn declaration to speak the truth in the Milosevic proceedings just as you did yesterday in these proceedings before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And during your testimony in the Milosevic proceedings, the transcript page 4047, lines 15 to 16, you confirmed that in addition to being a member of the KLA, you in fact at times were armed and in the field as a KLA insurgent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And are you telling us now that as an armed member of the KLA, you did not ever take part in the armed attacks undertaken by the KLA in Pristina against civilians?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither against civilians nor against armed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What specific KLA formation or unit were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a logistics unit or formation with its headquarters in Pristina and it was responsible for guerrilla duties in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say guerrilla duties, would that include guerrilla warfare?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact the KLA logistics base in Pristina had many members, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had several members.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, previously you mentioned that you had been to Drenica at some point in time and I believe you then clarified that you had been to several places as part of your duties as a member of the KLA. Isn't it a fact that sometime prior to the commencement of the NATO bombings in 1999, as part of your official duties within the KLA, you visited the KLA command in Drenica with several other prominent members of the KLA from Pristina, including representatives of the league of Albanian women and including your good friend Ms. Brovina; isn't that correct, and several others from Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And when we are talking about this KLA subgroup that was in the Pristina area, where, geographically, was the base located?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In several places but mainly at the clinic of Dr. Brovina, but also at other places in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you name the neighbourhoods in Pristina where the KLA was active or based, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no headquarters but there were groups of people who carried out different duties, to help with logistics, in several neighbourhoods of Pristina, Matrican, and Vellushi, Sofali, maybe in other districts or neighbourhoods as well but I can't remember all the neighbours now at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any KLA groups active in the Vranjevac neighbourhood, for instance the KLA group G-o-l-a-k?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many KLA groups were in Pristina but I know that there was a logistics group in Vranjevc [Realtime transcript read in error, "franities"].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that group in Vranjevac was preparing uniforms for the KLA fighters, was it not, among other supplies?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, yes, the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours I see a typographical error on the transcript page 19 line 14 it says "franities," which I believe the witness said "Vranjevac," which -- and I asked him a follow-up question, he confirmed, so I think it's pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Well, the witness said Vranjevc.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we are talking about the same place, is "Vranjevc" Vranjevac in Serbian, sir? I see you nodding your head. Is that a yes? We have to have an oral response.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you indicated that multiple groups were going around doing their different duties. I take it then those duties included organising and participating in terrorist attacks against the Serbian state. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think it was terrorists attacks against a state. This was open war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You do concede that the KLA, the group that you were a part of, in Pristina engaged in armed battles with components of the Serbian state, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what open war means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, what did you say, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I didn't catch the -- Your Honour, I said I thought that's what open war meant, engaging in armed battles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I thought so too but as you can see your witness seems to think otherwise so I'm trying to get clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, carry on, please, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. -- Dr. Kabashi, isn't it true that for the time period of 1998 through 1999 in and around the region of Pristina, that your KLA groups conducted guerrilla attacks in that region?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean guerrilla attacks and against whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Guerrilla attacks against anybody.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were guerrilla attacks, these guerrilla attacks were against military facilities and uniformed soldiers but I was not part of those groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But did you have knowledge of the activities that other members of your organisation were undertaking?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The group I was part of, with whom I worked, was mainly a group that dealt with logistics problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, logistics suggests to me that you are providing material supplies and material aid to active participating members of the KLA, and that your only reason for existing is to support armed activity. Now, have I got that wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But we could not supply the KLA with weapons because we couldn't, we didn't have those weapons, but we supplied them with things like paper or medicine or things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And not uniforms, which were raised earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, uniforms, but not weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Clothes, food, sanitary equipment, and other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was all that not done so that they could, in fact, carry out their armed activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, counsel is anxious to know whether you're aware that the KLA were carrying out attacks. Let's forget the fancy footwork around the words like "guerrilla" and "terrorist" and all the other words that seem to upset people in this courtroom, and let's just get down to basics. He wants to know whether you were aware that KLA people attacked other people in the Pristina area. Now, what's the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Pristina area, there was not such fighting. I have no information that the KLA attacked anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Was one of the other duties of your logistical unit preparing identification, IDs, for members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How about forging identity documents from humanitarian organisations to allow KLA fighters to pass freely through territories?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during your testimony at the Milosevic trial, you claim that reports about abductions of both Serbs and Albanians by the KLA were not true, that they were fabrications of the Serbian propaganda. Is that your -- is that accurate, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a page reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To this day, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We would all be helped by the page number. If that's a problem, it can be given later once someone assisting you has found it. But it does help if each time a quotation is selected from previous transcript, that we are given the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I apologise although the witness did confirm that was his testimony. That's at page 4041, lines 9 through 14 of the Milosevic transcript and I believe I can ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I accurate in stating that you -- your testimony is that reports of abductions of both Serbs and Albanians in 1998 were -- by the KLA were fabrications by the Serb propaganda? Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I take that to mean that the KLA did not engage in any policy or goal of abductions or kidnappings of any persons on the territory of Kosovo Metohija in either -- well, let's limit it to 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, so to my knowledge, this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've allowed that question to proceed to be answered, Mr. Ivetic, but really we don't have time, the luxury of the time necessary in this Tribunal to underscore a pretty clear answer several times over in the way that might be appropriate when you're putting something to a jury. I think we have to make more rapid progress through points like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will try to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The point I want to make, sir, is we have seen evidence here from the OSCE, that's the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe, and from Human Rights Watch, citing Adem Demaqi, the political spokesman of the KLA, among others, as stating that such abductions in fact were undertaken by the KLA during the relevant time period. How do you reconcile that fact with your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to ask Adem Demaqi about that. He is alive. You can call him to come here and he can testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I'm getting at, sir, is that much of your testimony is either inaccurate or biased in favour of the KLA. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that. That's an argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Pretty pointless question, Mr. Ivetic in the situation that we are in here. It's one that you might ask in other jurisdictions, I suspect but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perry Mason probably once got somebody to break down and admit to that but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: True enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, the fact that you are a member of the KLA, and from what you've testified to in the last two days, a fairly active member of the KLA, that appears nowhere in your sworn statement provided to the Office of the Prosecutor as part of these proceedings, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is there evidence that he was asked that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well there is a lot of confusion as to what he was asked and wasn't asked. We've received proofing notes from the Office of the Prosecutor, from Mr. Hannis, stating that he was present for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Ivetic, this falls into exactly the same category as the last. I mean -- it either is or it is not, and it will be clear from the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It goes towards confronting the witness and establishing whether in fact the witness has credibility or what probative value ought to be given to statements made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that depends whether the question was relevant to the interrogation that was taking place at that stage or whether it arose. You know, if you can show perhaps a part of the statement where inevitably that should have been said, then there might be something in your point but we don't know at this moment exactly what was being asked of him at that time and we know what he said in the Milosevic trial which is now, what, four years ago and more, and his motion was clear from then. So let's get to things that are material now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will do that, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to your statement and in the second paragraph of the statement which I believe is the second paragraph in all the various translations, you talk about policemen who you describe as having "military style" uniforms with White Eagles on their sleeves and berets. Is it your testimony that members of the Ministry of the Interior or MUP had such emblems on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can I direct your attention to the second paragraph of your sworn statement which is dated the 24th, I believe, of April, 1999 given to the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a hard copy we can hand the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say -- I did not say that these were --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. I have the English language version of that transcript -- of that statement in front of me. And in the middle of the second paragraph of that statement, in English it says, "There were police in standard uniforms, police in military-style uniforms, some of which had a White Eagle badge on their shoulders and a beret with a White Eagle badge." And I'm asking you, sir, if you -- first of all, now, since you've put that into doubt, did you in fact say that to the Office of the Prosecutor as part of your interview with them?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And my original question was is it your testimony that members of the Ministry of Interior had such emblems on their uniforms or are you talking about -- answer that question. Is it your testimony that members of the Ministry of the Interior or MUP had such --

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not say that and in fact I don't know what the MUP members had as their emblems. I don't know whether they were members of the police or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's clear enough answer. Now, you also claim in this paragraph that there were armed civilians. Did you see that with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only I saw them with my own eyes, but I felt it and -- because my house was attacked and everybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you're saying your house was attacked by armed civilians?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including armed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you stated that on the day of the 25th of March 1999, you received a telephone call from someone stating something to the effect of -- well, referencing NATO. I want to ask you about that telephone call. Did you perceive that as a threat against your life, some sort of reaction from somebody relative to the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I perceived that as a threat to my life, my family, and time proved that that was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you did not report this threat to your life and to your family to the police or other law enforcement authorities, did you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to ask you, were you there in Kosova in March 1999? Who could I report to? There was no police station. Everything was being carried out by the force of the gun and everybody was trying to shelter their families in the -- in a safe place where the guns could not reach them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I take that then that you did not report the threat to the police authorities. Am I correct in that assumption?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, surely you read that into that answer. This is another example of what I mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to make sure everything is clear and a simple -- I'm just asking for a simple yes or no answer. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you have to treat us as having a measure of common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the second paragraph of your statement, all versions, you talk about two policemen that you stated you knew from before, I believe Simic and Pedza are the names that you gave for them. Am I correct in understanding your testimony to be that you saw them patrolling the streets in the afternoon and that you did not see them take part in the attack against your home?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And near the middle -- near the middle of page 3 of the Albanian version of your statement, which is I believe paragraph 3 of page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S, you stated at the top -- that at the time of the explosion at your home, you told two other relatives in the room who were with you to lay down. Did you in fact also lay down to protect yourself?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sitting behind the door, having a telephone conversation when the bomb exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you remain in that position after the bomb exploded, sitting behind the door, having a telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Of course, not. I could not stay there sitting. The door fell on me. The telephone line was broken. Well, I think you can imagine what a bomb does when it explodes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can and that's why I asked if you were on the ground with your other family members after the bomb exploded.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say I was lying down, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, where exactly was this room located in relation to your house? For instance, what floor was it on?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the ground floor, on the right of the main door.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is your home surrounded by any walls or gates or other enclosures?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an iron gate, an iron fence around the yard at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was there any street lighting that was operative on that night, 25 March 1999?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There never was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what about inside your home? Was there any electricity in your home on that night, 25 March 1999, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The electricity was cut off at certain times, especially in parts that did not belong to the town. But this did not happen only that night. This happened all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that happened all the time after NATO started bombing, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before the NATO bombing there were many power cuts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe you set forth in your statement that after the explosion, there was a lot of smoke in the air from the explosive itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was it dark outside already when the event occurred? I believe you said it was 9.45 p.m. Was it dark at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when is the first time that you saw the vehicle that you first describe as a car and then as a jeep? That is to say, where were you when you first saw that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was inside my home and I went from room to room, as I told you, my mother was ill and I was doing errands, trying to help her. I saw it several times but I also saw it before dusk that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, would you concede that given the fact that it was dark outside, that there was no light either outside your home or inside your home, that there was dust and smoke in the air from the explosive, that you were, I would presume, emotionally quite traumatised by this occurrence, you would concede, would you not, that it would be very difficult for you to positively identify a dark vehicle in the dark night, would it not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the explosion at my house -- I don't know whether the vehicle was there but after the explosion and after the shots, there was this vehicle that came and part of the people who had surrounded the house got on to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you can not confirm that the vehicle took part in the explosive attack on your home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very narrow alley so I don't think the vehicle could get in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You state later in your statement, in the same paragraph, that on the Friday evening your house was burned. Now, you did not see the persons who burned your house or in fact how your house was burned, did you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, starting at the bottom of page 3 of the Albanian version of your statement and going on to the next page, page 3, paragraph 1 of both the B/C/S and the English versions, you list a series of deaths or killings of persons and I just want to make sure since it wasn't clear to me from reading it: You were not actually an eyewitness to any of these occurrences, were you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These events happened the next night, when I left Fushe Kosova. So during that night the people I mentioned here in my statement were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But you did not see any of those deaths. You only heard about them from others. Is that accurate, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I see them?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, in the next paragraph of your statement you talk about your stay in Dragodan which you claim was interrupted when army and special police broke down the door. Now, yesterday you conceded to my colleague that you had heard of paramilitaries misusing army uniforms and insignia and I'm asking you, did you also hear of and could the same be true for paramilitaries or criminals misusing police uniforms and insignia?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not heard about such misuse because I had no occasion, in no occasion did I hear about a distancing of these forces from the army and the police. They worked together. They acted together. It could have been misuse of uniform of a certain force or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You're speculating that you don't know. Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was a misuse of uniform or not, I don't know, because I did not deal in those things but I know that they cooperated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your interview on the 15th of August 2006 with Mr. Hannis and others from his office, I am told that you described the special police as having badges on their sleeves which stated, "Special police." Is it your recollection and your testimony that the badges of these persons you saw who broke into the door had the words in Serbian on their sleeves, "Specialna Policija"?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the initials that they had on their sleeves and we knew that they were the initials of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Which initials were there on the sleeve that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: SJ, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the next paragraph of your statement, you describe identity cards that you claim were taken from your wife and your sister-in-law, ripped and thrown on the floor, whereas another lady gave her card and it was given back to her. Did your wife and sister-in-law have valid official identification documents issued by the Serbian state or were their ID cards issued by the KLA or some other unofficial organ?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had official papers which were valid in Kosovo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were these documents issued by the Serbian state?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, one moment. At the end of March and beginning of April 1999, isn't it true that the KLA was present and actively opposing and fighting with Serbian forces in the neighbourhood of Vranjevc in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware whether it was them who fought in Vranjevc or Kodra e Trimave. What I know is, people fought to defend their own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are you aware of NATO bombs that fell on the neighbourhoods of Dragodan, Ciglani, and Vinogradi on March the 26th, 1999 and March 27th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there is a brick factory in Dragodan. I think that there are vineyards in Dragodan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe my question was, are you aware of any NATO bombs falling on the neighbourhoods of Dragodan, on the 26th of March and the 27th of March, first of all, and then I'll ask you about the others.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I recall your testimony you would have been in Dragodan around this time period. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is not Stara Ciglana another neighbourhood in that area of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I don't think it's a neighbourhood in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. We'll move on, then. Just a few more points that I want to clear up with you, sir. In paragraph 2 of page 8 of your statement, that's paragraph 2, page 5 of the English and the B/C/S, you stated that the police came and told you to leave the spot where you were standing because there was fighting in the middle of town in Dragodan and you might get hurt or killed. Now, what kind of uniform or insignia did this person that you identified as a policeman have or wear?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police had come to the whole neighbourhood, they were going from house to house forcing people out of their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically about the individual that told you that you had to leave the spot where you were standing because of fighting going on in the middle of Dragodan. What kind of uniform or insignia did this individual have?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I did not say that just one policeman came and told me this and that. But I said that we were forced out of our homes, we were told where to go, in the direction of the main street, because allegedly there was fighting and we were at risk and we -- you have to leave from this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Whoever told you this, what uniforms were they wearing? Describe them.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe these police uniforms for me? What colour were they?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policemen who forced us into the street, they had dark-coloured uniforms, police uniforms, almost black. They were masked and armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did they have any insignia on their sleeves?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did those uniforms differ from the standard uniforms of the police that you talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony then that all the police officers in Pristina wore these black -- almost black uniforms and were masked?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about all of them, but the one that I saw had such uniforms, while the soldiers had lighter coloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want you to focus on the policemen you were talking about because that's what you state in your statement. These policemen, what type of insignia or emblem did you see? Did these policemen have the same uniforms that you described earlier as belonging to the special police, the units you identified as the SJ?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, I saw three groups or police patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking about the police patrols. I'm asking about the --

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was the same uniform as the special police that you identified earlier with the insignia SJ on their shoulder? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see this SJ on the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You got that answer about two minutes ago, Mr. Ivetic. Quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: About the SJ. But is the uniform the same uniform as those uniforms that had an SJ on their shoulder is what I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've had that answer twice already, that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the general atmosphere in Pristina, especially after the NATO bombings. Would it be fair to say that there was a lot of open hostility from civilians, especially Serbs, towards Albanian civilians after the commencement of NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because at that time I did not pay attention to such cultural differences, whether there was enmity. So I cannot speak here about things that I have no information about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour, if I can refer to my notes, I think I'm done with the witness, and if I have one or two more questions I'd like to finish them before we take the break so, with your indulgence, I'll take a few moments to just look over my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm reminded of one series of questions. At the train station, what was the atmosphere like? Were there Serbian civilians harassing or verbally abusing the Kosovo Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see any. There weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you were at the train station for how long that day? Would it be most of the day? Do you have an approximation?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that day, but I stayed there for two or three days and three nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And during that time period you did not see any civilians -- you did not see any civilians at the train station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see any and I don't think there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what dates you were at the train station, sir?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th, 28th, and maybe 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for your time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Kabashi, you boarded the train in Pristina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did it travel through Fushe Kosova on the way to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There are no other tracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have maybe five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'd like you to continue with for the moment because it looks as though we may finish this witness in the next 15 minutes or so, and it would be convenient if we have a break around that stage because the next witness will be a protected witness who -- oh, no. Sorry. My mistake. Sorry, I'm running ahead of myself. There is no reason why we shouldn't take the break just now. So we'll break now and we'll resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, my name is Norman Sepenuk and my colleague here is Tomislav Visnjic and we are the attorneys for General Ojdanic. Good afternoon, sir. I have only a few questions for you and it's for purposes of clarifying the record because I think you can help us out here and enlighten us in a few areas and it has to do with some comments that you volunteered after you were being questioned by Mr. Fila here. Mr. Fila was questioning you, you remember, somewhat jocularly about when you graduated from college and how old you were and that sort of thing. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I finished my studies in 63, 1964 and I think I was 23 or 24 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm not asking about that. I'm just trying to get you back --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 73, 74.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's not important. I'm just trying to get you back into the context of your testimony. And right after that, after Mr. Fila finished with his questions, you said, and I'm quoting from the record now, "If I might, I would like to make a small explanation here. In the press in Belgrade and in Serbian TV, after the bomb was thrown into my house, they wrote that a certain terrorist was killed with my name and then with four children. It was also said a certain terrorist was killed with 11 members of his family, and another version which was on Tanjug was that a certain terrorist was killed with my name, with eight members of his family." So you recall that you testified to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And when you saw those articles and heard the -- what was said on -- or saw and heard what was said on Serbian TV, what was your reaction to those reports? Were you proud of being called a terrorist? Were you offended by being called a terrorist? Or maybe neither. Just tell us what your feeling was at that time when that press came out about you.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I laughed because I was used to such articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Have there been other articles about you in the Serbian press or the Kosovo press? Are you a person that the media writes about and knows about?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were articles from time to time but I haven't necessarily read them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Were there other articles that called you a terrorist?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So this was the first article to your knowledge that actually came right out and said that one Dr. Kabashi was a terrorist. Is that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the first article. They didn't say a certain Dr. Kabashi. They said Emin Kabashi was killed with four of his children and then there were the other versions too where my first and last name were mentioned with various numbers of children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. So I get back then to my question, and that is: What was your reaction to being called a terrorist? Pride? Were you offended? Neither? I want to hear your words, not mine.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I had no reason to be worried that -- by the fact that they were calling me a terrorist. I wasn't necessarily proud. All I did was laugh. And I was happy that I had survived the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So did the -- did the press and the media make a mistake when they called you a terrorist?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was a mistake. I was not a terrorist. I had never killed anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You weren't a terrorist but you were, as you put it in the Milosevic testimony, someone who saw that the only way for our people to win their freedom was by means of the gun, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to get back to the witness statement that was introduced in evidence in this case and I'd like to call your attention to the second paragraph of that statement, on page 2, and at that time you talked about being questioned by two Serbian police, Simic and Pedza. Do you recall that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the statement says, "Pedza took me in the police station about 4 a.m. one morning in 1998 to be interrogated with two plainclothes policemen I did not know. Two plainclothes policemen I did not know. I was accused of supplying the UCK with medicine and food. They kept me for seven hours." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what was your answer to the policemen, Pedza, to the question about whether or not you supplied the KLA with medicine and food?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policeman Pedza just took me to the station. The other two policemen of course I said I wasn't -- that wasn't -- I wasn't the person they were looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But I have a very specific question for you, and I'll say it again. According to this statement, you said that Pedza said you were accused of supplying the UCK with medicine and food. Okay? They accused you of it. Pedza accused you of it. What was your answer to Pedza at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was not the person who dealt with such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Was that true?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you lied to Pedza, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Because you were an operative with the Kosovo Liberation Army and you wanted to keep that secret. Isn't that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And how did you feel then, again getting back to that article in the press that took place right after the bomb was thrown, that you were suddenly revealed to the world as an alleged terrorist? What did that do to your effectiveness working within the KLA? Did you get comments about it or what happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. I didn't make any comment. I had no opportunity to comment the affair. There were no newspapers being published at the time and I had no opportunity to read all the newspapers in Belgrade and I wasn't really interested in dealing with comments, commentaries. I said maybe I laughed and I was happy that the news was not accurate, that I was in fact alive. It was not important to me at all, the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And how did you find out about those media reports and those press reports? When did those come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the articles was reproduced in an Albanian language newspaper in very briefly, on one of the days when there was a newspaper, and I was hiding with my family at the time and then I heard it on Tanjug, from Tanjug, from Belgrade, on TVS, and heard the news also on the Albanian media broadcasting from Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you would have heard all this shortly after the bomb was thrown on March 25th, 1999, you would have heard this within a few days thereafter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it three or four days after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were then interviewed on April 24th, 1999, about three weeks later, by Mr. Tim Kelly of the Office of the Prosecutor, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And we know that there is nothing specific in that statement about your membership in the KLA, correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you were -- in the latter part of that statement, actually on page 6, last paragraph, it says, "I have been asked specifically about the circumstances surrounding the time I was forced to leave Kosovo in March 1999. I have further information about events which happened at this time and prior to these events in Kosovo, and can provide if required." It's a fair reading -- that's a correct reading of your statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did it occur to you at all during that interview that your membership in the KLA might have been relevant to the questions that Mr. Kelly was asking you? Do you think he would have liked to have known that information?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't ask me about my activities and didn't -- I didn't give any responses about that. What I talked about were the events in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: He didn't ask you and you didn't think it was appropriate to volunteer any information to you -- to him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't consider that significant information, that is, my membership.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You didn't consider it significant to the objectivity of your statements to Mr. Kelly that you were really a rather high level operative in the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I object to the form of that question, Your Honour, a rather high level operative?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a foundation for that question, Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, I'm just trying to -- I'm just putting it into context of what's already been said, a long time member, a member of a group that supplied, you know, guerrilla fighters and that kind of thing. It's not essential to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's really not his evidence. It doesn't characterise it accurately, no. My impression, if anything, is the opposite. But there you go, it just shows you we can form different impressions. But I don't think there is a foundation for a question put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll modify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You didn't think that it would be relevant to the objectivity of the answers that you were given -- giving to Mr. Kelly that you were a member, high or low, of the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess my objection now is that he's asking him for a sort of legal conclusion about whether it was relevant or not. That's not an answer this witness is competent to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I could -- you know, Your Honour, I liked your comment about the fancy footwork before. Let's eliminate the fancy footwork.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Don't you think it was something that the investigators might have wanted to know, sir?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But you wanted to preserve your anonymity as a KLA member, did you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
