utterances.text: No, no, not at all. I just did my work as a citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell police officer Pedza the truth then when he asked you whether you supplied the UCK with medicine and food? We know from the testimony here that you did. Why didn't you tell him the truth?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not that much of a fool to spend the next ten years of my life in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you did want to a preserve your anonymity then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Sepenuk. Flogging and horse are springing to mind now. I think frankly you've exhausted this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. If I can get two more questions, Your Honour, along a different line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that had you been asked about potential crimes or crimes that had been committed by the KLA, that you realised that a witness who decides to testify against crimes committed by the KLA is at great risk?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't ask me and I don't have any information on such crimes. If I did have such information I would provide and say everything I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: To this day? Correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Who is -- do you know who Zekerijah Qana is?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Who is Zekerijah Qana?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zekerijah Qana was a professor of history at the Albanalogical institute. A specialist in history, a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was my professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And do you know him now? Do you have any relationship with him now?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We work together. We are colleagues at the same institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is he an honourable man, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need to object. We've gone well beyond two questions. I'm not sure where we are going with this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I can assure Your Honour I have a basis for asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can carry on for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is he an honourable man?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never thought about it in those terms. I don't see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, have you ever had any occasion to question the fact that he's a truthful man?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I've never dealt with such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm simply asking you whether you have any reason to think that your colleague or your professor is anything other than a truthful person. Very simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In my opinion he's answered that question, Mr. Sepenuk. There is no reason why he should ever have formed a judgement, according to his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If Mr. Qana made the statement that -- if he said this, "In Kosovo, every witness who decides to testify against the crimes committed by the KLA is at great risk," if Mr. Qana made that statement, would you believe that he was telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I never had occasion to deal with such matters or with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Mr. Hannis, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Chowhan has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Kabashi. Now, first thing relates to your name itself?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Do you know its meaning? Can you tell us the meaning of the word Kabashi? Or that's been a family name for a long time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean my first name? It means faithful, and my last name means that I'm from the region of Kabashi which is a geographical area between Shkodra and Ucin [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: That's very kind. My second question was, why were the gypsies with you at the relevant time, what you stated in your statement? The gypsies, why were they with you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were our neighbours for most of the time, and they were the families who refused to have their children sent to Serbian language schools and they were the ones who refused to dress up in uniforms of the police and to work for the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please tell me what was your subject in your doctorate?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject of my doctorate was the poetry of Jeronim De Rada, who was a major Albanian writer of the romantic period, and I endeavoured to underline the basic features of poetry in the romantic period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: That's very fine. Now, how were you attracted by the ideology of KLA? I mean, you were -- you're more towards romantic poet. I mean, how did this come in to attract you? And what was that philosophy?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't particularly attracted by the ideology of the KLA. I was attracted more by the ideology of freedom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Did you, sir, have a placement as an office bearer with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, okay. Could you tell us what was the manifesto or the motto with the KLA which attracted you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Freedom for Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, at one stage you were supplied with a list, you saw a list which contained names of different persons. What were the types of these -- what were the kind of these people -- what kind of people were being sought in that list?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they were activists, in logistics, or an intellectual. Some of them I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And last question is -- I'm sorry I've asked you so many questions. Last question is: In what activities were you indulging while with the KLA, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Things that had to do with the war, supplies of clothing, of food, of medicine, of movements, of helping the wounded, of mothers giving birth to children, helping people in general who were in a war situation or who were trying to get away from a war situation, and go somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So you remained there -- you did not move here and there, you remained there for these activities which you have pointed out. Or did you move to different places with the contingents or persons?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I moved from time to time to carry out certain duties which I could not carry out in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kabashi, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I want to address just Defence counsel in very general and gentle terms at this stage. We've now had evidence from a number of witnesses who are speaking about the events on the ground in Kosovo, how they affected them and how they affected other people. And you've had an opportunity to assess the results of cross-examination of these witnesses and you must now have a feel for what's the way in which to obtain the most important information from the cross-examination of these witnesses. What I hope you'll do in the light of that is assess the situation to try to judge what questions are essential, what are important, and what questions are of marginal importance. I'm beginning to feel that we need to prune some of the cross-examination, but I equally remain convinced at the moment that it's best to place faith in your judgement rather than to take any particular measures to deal with it. Now, obviously, if you need more time to come to a better evaluation of how to perhaps prune the cross-examination, then obviously the Bench accept that we are in the early days of the trial still and that it may be necessary to allow time to do that but I hope you'll begin that exercise now and with a view to seeing if we can't accommodate perhaps a few more witnesses in the course of a month than it looks as though we are likely to do at the moment. Now, Mr. Ackerman, you want to raise something to do with the way in which evidence is presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is, and I think I speak for all or most of my colleagues at this point, we try to prepare far enough ahead so that we are ready for any witness that comes into the Court so we presume a certain amount of time for each witness based upon what the Prosecution thinks they will take and what we believe cross-examination will take. And so we are not prepared for every witness that might be called and we couldn't possibly be. It creates complete havoc in our preparation when we come into court like today and learn -- I learn for the first time the Prosecution changed the order of witnesses. So witnesses that I'm prepared for have now been moved down, witnesses I'm not prepared for have been moved up. And I understand there was an e-mail that some of my colleagues got around noon advising of that but I didn't learn of it until I came into court because I did not look at my e-mail around noon. My e-mail system was not working or I would have, but it was broken down and I think you have to allow nor e-mail systems being broken down occasionally even. Mine certainly breaks down more often than it should. So that's one of the problems. The second one is with regard to the next witness in this case. I think we were all handed an envelope when we came here into this courtroom at 2.15. I know I was, and I think I observed everyone being handed the envelope of new disclosure materials. And in the new disclosure materials are a statement from the witness that's coming and supposed to come right now, at least I'd never seen it before now and I don't think anyone else has either. I think it was given to us for the first time today. So I feel very uncomfortable in trying to engage in a cross-examination of that witness within the next few minutes without having had at least a minimum of 30 to 45 minutes to consider the effect of that new statement, which I've not had, and I'm sure that some of my colleagues are learning just now about that new statement just by hearing me say it because they haven't opened up their packet and looked at it and seen that's what was in it. But that's what was in it. It's a new statement from the next witness. Not a new statement. I think it was an older statement that was just disclosed. But those are problems and those are problems that -- they go to exactly what you were just saying, that sometimes we might need more time to prepare. It's been my observation over the years, both from this side of the Bench and sitting up there that prepared lawyers tend to move at a faster speed and more efficiently and unprepared lawyers. Unprepared lawyers tend to flop around a lot and take a bunch of time that's unnecessary. I would encourage you to give us an opportunity to be as prepared as we can. I think we will move faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll make no comments on the last observation but on the material, are you referring to a statement taken on the 16th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know. It's on a disk, and I'm not sure of the date. What was not taken here. It was taken in some other location. And it was taken on 17 May -- no, 14 April of 1999. So this statement has existed for a very long time. I don't know why it just got around to getting to us today but that's when it was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: If I may assist with that. We disclosed these notes. These are internal investigator's notes of an interview that was done in the camp in Macedonia with this witness in 1999. We have not previously disclosed these notes because it's not an interview, as we consider it, and it's not a statement. We have now disclosed them only for the sake of completeness and the Defence would see if they compare the statement from the statement the witness later gave to an investigator of the ICTY, and these notes that another investigator took a couple of years ago, that they are actually reflecting the same thing. And we disclosed that not under Rule 66(A)(i) as a statement but only for the sake of completeness and because the issue of disclosure of whatever information we have relating to a witness was an issue recently with other witnesses, we did so. We don't consider this to be a statement of the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it doesn't record what he said?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It records what the investigator talking to the witness took down at that point. That was when he first talked to her. It's just a bullet point summary, and until we had this discussion the other week here in the court we always considered that internal documents, working documents of the OTP. We have now adopted the practice be -- to disclose fully whatever we have but under the -- under the legal assumption that this is not falling under Rule 66(A)(i) or [ii].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem is quite simply that when you hand over stuff immediately before the witness is going to give evidence then you inevitably encourage the sort of submission that we have just received. And it's surprising that you should be doing that when at the end of last week you were able to notify us of an up-to-date statement taken from the same witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, the statement taken on 16 August we had immediately translated and disclosed to the Defence and this is what we consider her statement, the addendum to her first statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All I'm saying is it would have been helpful to have disclosed the other one at the same time. But as it is, we get it today and at least I haven't seen it at all but Defence counsel have got it and they are concerned that they should have time to consider its implications. Perhaps I could see it and then I might be in a position to make a better judgement on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. We will certainly try to get a copy to the Court. We haven't sent it to the Court yet because it is not something that we want to tender or something that we consider a statement. It's not signed. It wasn't read back to the witness. There isn't even the name of the investigator on that. It's just an internal document that we found in our files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're fortunate because before cross-examination takes place, there no doubt will be another break or at least it will be very early in the cross-examination and that half-hour break will give at least Mr. Ackerman the length of time he requires to, as a minimum, to consider the position. And it may be then he'll be able to do it in the light of the evidence of the witness as well. Now, the second point that is made is that changing the order of witnesses is unhelpful and, if possible, something to be avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with that but I would indicate to the Court part of the reason that we find that necessary to do is because we don't know how long the preceding cross-examination is going to take with witnesses because sometimes that's taken much longer than estimated. We have witnesses who have obligations, who have to return sooner, so we have to shift the order to move somebody up so they can get back to Kosovo on time for some previously scheduled operation or some appointment or some other business, and they have been here waiting maybe five days before they get on. We've tried to minimise that as much as possible but given the current circumstances that has arisen a couple of occasions. And right now we are dealing with witnesses that are fairly simple. One order that we changed with K 62 and 36, whose evidence is closely related and should not pose any great difficulty in doing one before the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, is there anything else to be said at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I just learned from a colleague that there is also an addendum to her statement that I've not -- that I don't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that was intimated on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That may be my fault that I didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Late on Friday but it was on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've not seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that will give you any great difficulty. It may raise matters that you want to look into but that's a separate issue that we couldn't deal with at this minute any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. Your next witness, then, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we call Mrs. Nazlie Bala as our next witness. We call her under Rule 92 bis (B) and her evidence relates to paragraph 72(G) and 77(A) of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Bala.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you now make the solemn declaration please by reading aloud the document which will be placed in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat. Now, Ms. Bala, we have before us principally a statement which you gave to the office of the Prosecution here in June 2001. We have certain other written material so we know a lot about the evidence that you are giving. The purpose of this afternoon's attendance at court is to enable further questions to be asked by the counsel representing the Prosecution and representing the various accused. These questions will vary greatly. Some will be to challenge what you said. That's part of the process under which we operate. Others will be to amplify or clarify. The important thing is that you concentrate on the particular question that is asked and try to confine your answer to the particular issue that's raised in the question. The first person to ask questions of you will be on behalf of the Prosecution, Ms. Moeller. Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Bala. Could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: My name is Nazlie Bala. I was born in Pristina in May 1967. I finished my secondary education --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you but please try to just answer the concrete question and I will take you step by step, if that's possible. Yeah? Ms. Bala, where did you live in 1999?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: In 1999 I was living in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 30 June 2001?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you given an addendum to the statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 16 August 2006?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could the usher please take the statement to the witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, can you have a look at that statement and tell if this is your statement and your addendum to the statement?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. And can you confirm to the Court that this is a correct and -- a correct statement and your evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes. I take full responsibility when I say that this is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point we would like to tender the statement. It has Exhibit number P02262.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that number also apply to the addendum?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, it's all in one package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Bala I would like to take you to some points of your statement and your addendum to the statement, step by step. In paragraph 3 of your addendum, you set out a little bit about your professional background and I would like to ask you to tell the judges a little bit about your professional experience just in a few sentences.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I finished my secondary school in Pristina, also the university in Pristina. Now I'm doing my masters degree in international relations and cultural competences -- cultural affairs, and from 1997 [as interpreted] I have been working for the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in Kosovo, focusing on violence against young people, women, and children. By the end of 1998, I joined the OSCE mission in the Pristina, the office for human rights. In the beginning, I was part of the main department, but in two or three weeks -- two or three weeks later I started working in the regional office, what was called RC 5 Pristina, until the 20th of March 1999. After the 20th of March, I went to Macedonia. I was a refugee but I still worked for the OSCE mission in the refugee camps in Cegran, Neprosten, Sanokos, Stenkovec, 1, 2, 3, in Ohrid, Dibra, and other places in Macedonia. After I went back to Kosovo, I was the first local staff member that joined the OSCE mission team. I think this was about 15th of -- or 16th of June 1999. I continued working for them until September 1999, department of human rights. I worked mainly on mass graves in various locations in Pristina and around Pristina. In October 1999 I started working as a coordinator of NGOs dealing with human rights until 2001, June 2001, when I started my studies and that takes us to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, one point that perhaps you can clarify. Your statement before us or the addendum to it says that you started to work for the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in 1989.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I started in 1989 when this organisation was founded in Kosovo, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be a translation but you've just been recorded as saying that you started in 1997. Any way, you've confirmed the accuracy of the written statement. Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, regarding your work for the OSCE that you addressed, do you know Sandra Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, Sandra Mitchell was the director for the department of human rights in the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you state in your addendum that you took about 300 interviews for the OSCE; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. In the course of my work for two months and a half in Macedonia, working for the OSCE mission, during that time, I took about 300 statements from various witnesses. I say approximately 300.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that relates to paragraph 5 of the addendum.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, can you tell the Judges a little bit about how these statements were taken?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: The work --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would object at this point and ask the other -- my learned colleague from the other side whether these statements have been disclosed to the Defence or not, if she inquires regarding these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if she declines to answer that question at the moment, I -- it wouldn't surprise me because that's the question is simply related to the methodology. Whether it's going further than that remains to be seen. Do you want to deal with the matter, Ms. Moeller, or do you want to continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to continue because this is firsthand experience of the witness herself, how she took statements like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Lukic will no doubt renew this objection when you get to the point, if you get to the point of trying to lead evidence about the contents of these statements. Is that what you propose to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's not where I'm going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think, Mr. Lukic, at the moment you're that's premature. You can see if anything that you ought to object to does arise. Carry on for the moment, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, as I asked you could you describe to the Judges how you would take such statements for the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, the OSCE mission in Macedonia, especially the human rights department, worked directly with its teams on the ground in the refugee camps. I worked in Cegran, Sanokos, Stenkovec, 1, 2, and 3, but we also went to the houses where refugees were sheltered. The teams that took statements were very professional and experienced. In each of these camps, we had our tents. There were tents in these camps and we went from one tent to another to get the information, what happened to those people, until the point when they reached the refugee camps in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And before you started conducting interviews for the OSCE were you given a training how to do such interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm really sorry I have to interrupt again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We received from the OTP the summary of what this witness should be testifying about and in this summary I cannot find anywhere that this witness will describe the methodology regarding these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the addendum to the statement in paragraph 4 and paragraph 5 deals with her work for the OSCE and it mentions that she was personally involved in the interviews of 300 witnesses so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not Mr. Lukic's point. Mr. Lukic's point is that there is a procedure to be gone through for disclosure that involves the application of rules and you have -- you were bound to summarise the evidence of this witness which you've done and this is not part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We think it is covered by paragraph 4 and 5 in the addendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. We're talking about 65 ter at the moment. You've got an obligation in your summary -- you've got an obligation under Rule 65 ter to summarise the evidence of a witness and there is no hint in your summary, according to Mr. Lukic, that this witness will give evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I now see your point, Your Honour. The fact is we sent out this notification including the 65 ter summary before we had the witness actually present for proofing, and it only turned out during the proofing. And this is why we put it in the addendum statement at the point which was disclosed and translated for the Defence in time that we included it there. So it's not in the 65 ter summary because we did not have a possibility to inquire into this area with her any earlier before she came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you mean you didn't take the opportunity to inquire of her any earlier. But -- which is rather different.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: If I may add one thing, Your Honour? The fact that Ms. Bala worked for the OSCE and for quite a while is contained in her very first witness statement and first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm looking for the bit that says that she did anything between March and June 1999. I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. This is only in the addendum statement, that's correct, Your Honour. We gave the notice as soon as we found out from the witness during the proofing that she did this additional work in the addendum statement and we considered this to be appropriate disclosure at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, we have never seen this addendum because we were not looking for it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour may I add, just for additional information, we never received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Visnjic. I'm trying to understand something at the moment. Yes, Mr. Lukic, what was it you wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Yes. I wanted to add that this addendum was placed on the e-court but we have never been formally informed about it. So we were not aware, I personally was not aware of it five minutes ago. Our case manager just showed me a few minutes ago that there is an addendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes. The procedure so far was as follows.. The Prosecutor would inform us about an addendum or any other information through e-mail or any other way. We would get information either in writing or via e-mail but this time we did not receive any information. I found out just now that it was on e-court. At this point in time it doesn't mean a thing to me if I don't at least get an e-mail saying that it's on e-court. Mr. Ackerman already explained that during the weekend we really have a problem because we do not have proper access. Mr. Petrovic reminded me just now if something new appears on e-court we do not have this information. We have to have a look at everything that's on e-court but we don't know what the most recent things are. It would have been logical for us to receive at least information via telephone or via e-mail, and I assume that they expect us to do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I only really want to hear from other counsel if there is something to be added to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is, just to further complicate matters. I was struggling to work with e-court on Sunday and it completely went down very early Sunday and stayed down all night. It didn't come back up until 8.00, 7.30, 8.00 Monday morning because they were doing maintenance on it or something. Had it completely shut down, so you couldn't get in at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That sounds irrelevant to the point being made at the moment, which is you wouldn't know any way even if you went into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you went into e-court and looked up this exhibit and looked at it, you would find that addendum on the end. But there was no notice otherwise that it was there. You would only find it by accident if you did that, and that's if you had lost the disclosure they gave you earlier which most of us probably didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Only point I wish to make and I think it was alluded to previously and I won't go further if it's clear to the Bench but in my submission this procedure, this practice, is a violation of Rule 65 ter and the Prosecution's pre-trial brief in which the Prosecution must provide a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify. Now, this trial, this matter has been in pre-trial for four years and we sat in status conference after status conference, where there is no new Rule 66 disclosure, everything's been disclosed to us. We sat through that for years, and now in addition to the summary that was included in the pre-trial brief now we are developing a practice where there is new statements, new addendums, new information. That's highly unfair and it's a violation of the rule under a pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How does one deal with it, though, if it is genuinely material that comes to light at the last minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there is an obligation on the Prosecution to prepare its case. The pre-trial brief puts this case in trial ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Answer, you know, humour me by answering the question I'm asking you. I understand entirely the point you're making but there will be examples of information genuinely coming to light at the last minute. Now, how do you deal with the fact that it's not in a 65 ter summary, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At a minimum there must be a showing of good cause on the party that is bringing this new information. They must show due diligence that they pursued all information, that it was good cause, that something arose at the last minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That suggests then that there should be an application.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because there has been a failure to comply with the strict terms and for some sort of modification or at least for the allowance of a late addition to the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller do you want to add anything before we deal with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like to add that we were just trying to find out what happened with this addendum, and at this point we cannot find that it went out by e-mail, indeed, which is normally the practice in this case and there were clear instructions that it should go out as soon as it was processed in our system. So it appears at this point that indeed there was no e-mail notice to the Defence in this case, which is very unfortunate and I apologise. That's what I want to add at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there are two separate issues here. The addendum does appear to be genuinely that, and is simply a modest amplification of the information contained in the statement. It tells more about the background and experience of the witness, and that's something that one would not expect any more to be said in a 65 ter summary. On the other hand, the matter now being dealt with is a quite separate issue and of some importance in view of objections already taken to evidence in the case and in relation to that matter currently under active consideration by the Bench. Where there is nothing in the existing material to herald that a witness will be asked questions of such significance to an important issue in the trial, then it's necessary for the party leading the witness to take steps to seek relief from the failure to comply with 65 ter, and that, as a starting point, requires, as Mr. O'Sullivan has indicated, a showing of good cause and that requires to be done in the form of an application to the Trial Chamber. Such an application could, of course, be made orally, but would probably, to give the Defence adequate notice, normally be made in writing. In relation to this point, that is the actual -- or the way in which, the methodology by way these statements were taken, this was no notice given to the Defence and no attempt made to seek relief from the Trial Chamber for failure to notify that in the 65 ter list and summary, and nothing has been said. Today amounts to good cause but, of course, no doubt that's because the issue hasn't been particularly considered. So in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, it would certainly be unfair to the Defence to allow further evidence from this witness on the methodology and therefore her evidence will be confined to issues of which notice has been given. Of course, if the Prosecution were to feel that an adequate explanation could be offered to the Trial Chamber and that it was essential to lead this evidence from the witness, then they could at a later stage seek the relief that we've indicated will be necessary in such circumstances and bring the witness back for that purpose. But as the matter has been presented to the Defence, it would in our opinion be unfair to proceed further with that part of her evidence at this stage. We therefore confine it to what has been intimated in the 65 ter summary. Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to clarify, regarding other issues in the addendum statement, we would be allowed to lead evidence on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's already in without objection. Perhaps you were lucky but it got there. And just looking at it, it does clarify the main statement and doesn't appear to do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's why not only is it evidence because it's already in, but in addition, we have made it clear that if you had sought against objection to have it allowed in, then we would have allowed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't leave the record saying that it's just a clarification. There is one point in it where she makes a complete change in what she said in a prior statement on an issue of significance, which I will probably raise during cross-examination. But there is -- it's more than clarification in that, at least one instance and maybe more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But when a witness, Mr. Ackerman, says something different from what was said before, that is clarification. In fact it's essential that that should be brought to the attention of everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just think it's more than clarification, it's substantive change in the statement. That's the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What are you referring to? I mean, it's a matter for you whether you want to tell me at this stage because it's -- it's not going to change our mind but it may help us to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd be happy to tell you when the witness is not listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I mean. So you can deal with it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In clarification to your statement, Ms. Bala, let me take you to 26 March 1999. You say in your statement that you took some observations on this day and that you kept a lookout and observed things in the neighbourhoods of Dragodan, Kodra e Trimave, Vranjevc, Taslixhe, and Kolovica. Could you explain to the Chamber how you were able to make your observations and from where?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: In my statement of 26th of June 1999, I observed from three angles and I could observe Dragodan, Kodra e Trimave, otherwise called Vranjevc, and Taslixhe and Kolavic. My house is in the old part of town, Pristina. It's five-storey house. There is no roof, but the building has a big terrace, and from the terrace I could see these four places. And I could see them very well. I could see the movements of the people, what was happening. Whenever it was difficult for me to see, I used binoculars in order to be able to observe what was happening in various parts of Pristina. I couldn't observe other parts of Pristina that were far away from where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we please put up Exhibit P0013 on the screen. It's a map of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's P13.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we have to clarify something. Maybe it's just a mistake but I just learned, or it appears that way, the witness said, page 69, line 4, "in my statement on 26th of June 1999." We have never seen this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can I clarify this with the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, did you understand what the Defence counsel just said? You referred to a date of 26th of June or at least the transcript reads of that. Have you given a statement at that day or are you referring to your statement of 30 June 2001 and 16 August 2006?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: The 26th, I was speaking about the observations of the event of -- that happened on the 16th -- sorry, on the 26th of June 1999 [as interpreted], and those are reflected in my statement, and I gave this statement also in July and June of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I have to ask you again because the transcript now reads that you speak about the events on 26 of June 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: That was 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay so the interpreter corrected. It was an interpreter's correction. I think that clarifies this question, I hope, sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You said you had a good view from the roof of your house. Which area was your house located at? How was it called?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: The building where I lived is Ruga e Llapi, number 30. It is in the old part of town, close to the old market of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Would that be in the centre of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: No. It is not in the centre of Pristina. It's in the northwestern part of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we maybe zoom in a little bit on this map so that the witness can have a look?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: If you could take the -- could you take it a little bit higher? Even more. If you could stop there. My house is approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could you mark it with the pen that the usher is giving to you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: It's not very clear. These are various parts of Pristina. My house is here. From my house I could see Dragodan, Vranjevc, Kolovica, which is behind my house, and Taslixhe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we please take a snapshot of it and assign it an IC number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit IC 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Moeller, we will have to have another break here. Do you think your examination will be long?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I think I will be done in 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I continue with Ms. Bala could I ask for an indication that any possibility that the next witness could actually start today? Because if not we would release him for today. He's waiting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. O'Sullivan is usually the man to tell us if there is significant cross-examination to be anticipated.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At this point, it's not significance. We don't anticipate it would be significant at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if cross begins about 6.15 or 6.20, should we keep the next witness? No is the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the witness may be excused and if would actually help greatly if we finished this witness tonight because further arrangements have to be made for the evidence of the next witness and they can be dealt with so that we start and don't lose time in the morning. So please carry on, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Ms. Bala, before the break we talked about 26th of March 1999. And you mentioned that you could see VJ, MUP and Serb civilians destroying Albanian houses and Albanian shops in your statement. Could you please explain, how could you distinguish that it was VJ, MUP and Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: I live in Kosova, I was brought up there, and so I know quite well how to distinguish between policemen and soldiers and civilians. The army had dark green uniforms, the police had blue, dark blue camouflage uniforms, and the civilians from time to time wore police jackets, vests, and they sometimes had various arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let me take you now to the 29th of March. That was the day when you were expelled from your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You mention in your statement that a VJ officer and a gypsy came to your house. Do you know who that gypsy was?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was Ivica was his name. I don't remember his last name. He lived in town. His house was in my neighbourhood. He worked as a traffic policeman and was responsible for that area where we lived, for the neighbourhood we were living in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, you explain in your statement that you were taken to the train station, boarded a train and that this train at some point arrived at the border crossing of Hani i Elezit and in your statement you say that Serb forces were standing guard over you and the others there. Could you explain what you mean by "Serb forces"?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: It was an afternoon and it's hard to remember things, the exact time of things, but I think it was about five in the afternoon when we arrived at the train station in Pristina, and from the morning until that time we had been walking through the streets of Pristina, all the time, everywhere the train stopped in Fushe Kosova and Lipijan [phoen], Ferizaj, Hani i Elezit, we could identify on all the stations that there were policemen or paramilitaries or soldiers. All the time the barrels of the rifles were pointed towards us, towards the train, that is, for the whole period, during all the stops of the train, we were not allowed to look at them directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this isn't even remotely responsive to the question. The question was, "What do you mean by Serb forces." She's telling a story. It has nothing to do with the question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I disagree with that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, just a minute. Look at it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She just said -- the question was, "Could you explain what you mean by Serb forces?" And then she tells the whole story about her today and never says anything about what she meant by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not responsive. It's simply not responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hear you Mr. Ackerman. Please carry on now and deal with the question, Ms. Bala.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, during the whole time and the stops that we made in Fushe Kosova, Lipijan, Ferizaj, Hani i Elezit, the train was surrounded by Serb forces. Police, army and forces who I had never seen in my whole life before, in Pristina at least. These forces were -- had black uniforms with the flags, with white, red, blue flags, and they had insignia on various parts of their uniforms. They were Serb uniforms. They were police, army, and these other forces, who were not part of the logo -- of the legal forces of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did the forces that you just described work together? Did you see them together?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes. In all the places we stopped, everywhere where the train stopped, all these forces were together.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Bala, one last question from my side. Did you leave Pristina and Kosovo because you were afraid of NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Both I and my family, none of us left Pristina because of NATO bombing. We left -- we were forced to leave by the army, the police, and these other forces who were present in Pristina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No further question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller. Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions. We'll proceed in this order: General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, General Lukic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a day of surprises, Your Honour. I'm surprised at the order in which we are doing cross-examination. It's different from what I had requested?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I was nominated, I guess, to go first, and I guess I'm prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's just one of those days where nothing seems to work the way it is supposed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I intervene. I want to share with you something that's regarding the meaning of the name. "Bala" means somebody above everybody else in Persian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, Ms. Bala, my name is John Ackerman, I represent General Pavkovic. I have a few questions to ask you and if you try to listen to the question and answer it as precisely as possible, we'll finish quicker. One thing I've noticed about you today, just watching you, is you are a person who is I think quite intelligent and also a person who is extremely careful with regard to the things you say and the things you do, and one of those observations was when you were handed your statement and asked to tell us whether or not it was your statement you very carefully went through it to check it to just absolutely be certain that when you said it was your statement, it was your statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's that same kind of care with which you've gone through the process of making your statements in this case, in giving your testimony here today, I take it?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talk about working for OSCE there in Pristina until OSCE departed Kosovo. You obviously didn't go with them and stay with them when they left. Were you asked to accompany OSCE or did that end your job with them at that point?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: When the OSCE mission was evacuated, all the local staff was offered a possibility to be evacuated with the mission to Macedonia, because they were afraid that their local staff would be a target for arrest, for killings, for kidnappings, and such things, and I was given the opportunity to leave but I was with my family, I had my family there and wanted to be with my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the OSCE evacuated out of concern for the danger that might be coming up and offered the opportunity for anybody else that worked for them to leave with them? Fair statement?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: As I said, local staff were given the opportunity to leave, and I was given that offer too but I did not accept it. But I say once again that the OSCE did offer this possibility to all its local staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's how we waste time, because you simply gave me the same answer twice. You could have just said yes, I think. Along that line, you gave a statement to the OTP on 30 June 2001, and that statement was reduced to writing in English. It was read to you and translated into your language, and after you had carefully considered its accuracy, you signed it, said it was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection, and you signed your name to each page of it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the process of being extraordinarily careful about it being accurate and saying what you -- really is the truth, you certainly heard that in that statement you had said, "I spoke with a number of the Albanian civilians who told me that they were preparing themselves for a Serb invasion and because of this fear they were sending their families out of Pristina." That was there, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: During my preparations for my arrival here in The Hague, I think I discovered a misunderstanding. I didn't want to say that the people were preparing themselves for an invasion. What I meant was that they didn't know what to do. I think that was a misunderstanding between me and the person I gave the interview to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you were given an opportunity to clarify that misunderstanding when it was read over to you and you were asked if it was true to the best of your knowledge and belief, and you said yes and signed it, didn't you? You can say yes or no to that.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were given an opportunity to clarify the misunderstanding that you say existed there when that statement was read over to you and you were given an opportunity to clarify it and you did not do so. You said it was true to the best of your recollection and belief and you signed it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you signed the very page upon which this language appears, didn't you? The bottom right-hand signature, that's yours, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you came here and gave this addendum to the Prosecutor on August whatever you did that, August 16th, I guess it was, that you gave this addendum to the Prosecutor, you then said that what appeared in that paragraph 4 wasn't really the case, that when on 20th March you spoke to these people in the Albanian community, these civilians, they didn't tell you that they were preparing to send their families from Pristina. So you changed it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: I said that there was a misunderstanding here or misunderstanding as to how they interpreted my English because I gave the statement in English. It was simply a misunderstanding. I said they were afraid for their families, of what would happen to them, but I didn't mean that the families were preparing to send their members away. It was simply a misunderstanding during the interpretation of my English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you gave this statement in English, then I suspect you had an opportunity to read it in English before you said it was true and correct and signed it. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I did have an opportunity to read it and see it. I can only say once again that there was a misunderstanding here. It was my mistake for not having seen that. I did not mean that families were preparing to send their family members away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably was. So was it read to you -- was it read to you in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: The statement in Pristina was read over to me in English as I gave it, whereas the statement here in The Hague was given in Albanian, and that's probably the origin of this misunderstanding between the two languages on the one word here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So at the end of that statement that you gave in Pristina, which bears your signature and a date, I think probably written in there by you, where the acknowledgement says "the six-page statement has been read over to me in the Albanian language," that's also not true? Another mistake, right?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you got your statement there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at the last page called witness acknowledgement. It says, "This six-page statement has been read over to me in the Albanian language." And then you signed that. And now what you're saying is that's also not true, that it was read to you in English, correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: The statement in Albanian was the one I read here in The Hague, whereas the one in English was the one I read in Pristina at the time I gave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please listen carefully to the question you're being asked and try to answer that particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question I asked you was the statement in Pristina -- I don't care about the one here, the statement in Pristina that you're looking at right now, says, "This six page statement has been read over to me in the Albanian language." And right below that is your signature and the date written in, I think by you, and now you're saying that's also not true, that it wasn't read to you in the Albanian language in Pristina and so you've signed another untruth. Is that what you're saying to us?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: No. I never said anything untruthful in the statement. I think there is simply confusion here. The statement in Albanian is the one I gave here in The Hague, and that was where I read it here in Albanian. I don't know which of the declarations you're talking about. I read it over and it's the same and nothing was added to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That can't be right. You're being asked to look at a specific page of the statement, the statement you gave on the 30th of June 2001. And at the end of that there is a witness acknowledgement. Now, it says, "This six page statement has been read over to me in the Albanian language." And the point that's being made to you is that that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Six years is enough time to recall all these events. If that's what I declared, on this last page, that must mean that I read it over in Albanian. It must be true. There must have been a confusion here because I didn't see the last page here. I did give my statement directly in English but it's been so many years, so much time has gone by that I'm not sure whether they read it back to me in English or in Albanian but I do know that I went through the statement and verified the whole statement. I'm sorry if there is confusion here. I can't remember exactly how it was. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with that completely. Six years ago you went through it very carefully and what you said then was true. Obviously it was true. You may have forgotten since then. So when you said then, "I spoke with a number of the Albanian civilians who told me they were preparing themselves for a Serb invasion and because of this fear they were sending their families out of Pristina," that was true and you've just forgotten since then. And you gave a statement here the other day that was wrong, correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: What I discussed with the people that I met is true, and I will never forget what they told me. I will never forget their fear, their horror, the expression on their faces. Please let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, you have to answer the question. I asked you a question. Please answer the question I asked you. Don't give a speech.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: I'm not giving a speech. I'm simply explaining what happened. The Albanians I talked to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I -- again I disagree with your approach to this. I do not think that the witness is straying beyond the bounds of what's a reasonable way to answer the question you're putting to her. Now, carry on, please, and answer as best you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the conversations I had on the 20th of March 1999, when I went into town to various parts of Pristina, I talked to a lot of people, and on their faces I could see the horror, the fear, everything. Their fear and horror was for what might happen to their families because they were left to the mercy of fate. They were not prepared for the situation. They were not prepared to send their families away. They didn't know what to do with them. This -- these conversations I can remember vividly even today because I was just as horrified for them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these conversations were on the 20th of March, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you remember them vividly today, as you've just told us.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Those events, the horror, the fear, is alive in the minds of all Albanians, not only in my mind, and even if you call me here 700 years from now, I will be here to testify, if I am alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question was: You remember them vividly today just as you remembered them vividly when you gave your statement in Pristina in 2001. You couldn't have gotten that wrong because you remembered it so vividly. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: I remember the events very well, and I have the whole thing before me eyes. These were events that had to do with life or death so these are events that cannot be forgotten. I told you earlier that this might have been a mistake on my part, an oversight on my part, but I stand by my statement, the things that I've said there, and I will say these same things in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you want to tell us how horrible everything was and how terrible everything was and what a horrible time this was and I agree with all that. So I don't need you to tell me that over and over and over, and I think the Chamber understands that. What I do need you to do is try to answer just a question. And when we asked you about your witness acknowledgement that says it was read over to you in the Albanian language, you said, well, I guess I'm wrong, at the time it probably was read over to me in Albanian. I'm sure I wouldn't have made a mistake then. So when I then go to paragraph 4 and say, well, based upon that you certainly didn't make a mistake in that paragraph either, especially when this is -- these events are so vivid to you. Now, I don't know why you can't just answer me whether that was true or not at the time you made it. Did you look at it and consider it when you signed that paper and say it was true? That's what I'm trying to get you to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I signed this statement on the 16th of August 2006, and in June 2001, then everything is correct. I mean the statement in English and the other one in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So everything is correct in both of them? Yes?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me suggest to you, and you'll have a chance to answer me, let me suggest to you that you changed your statement here in paragraph 7 of your addendum because what you had said in your Pristina statement, that you spoke to a number of civilians on March 20th who were preparing themselves for a Serb invasion and because of their fear they were sending their families out of Pristina, you realised that that was not politically correct, that the political line must be that nobody left voluntarily. And so you changed it when you came here, didn't you? Isn't that what you did? And what you said here in this statement is not true.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Sir, what I discussed with these people -- maybe it is necessary for me to repeat this again, the conversation with them was about their fear, they feared what would happen with their families. They were not preparing to send their families outside Kosovo. Maybe it was a mistake on my part. I did not explain -- I did not read this in detail. Maybe it was an oversight, but the meaning is there. They feared for the future of their families, for the life of their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm finished with that area and I want to talk to you about something else. A major part of what you've told us in your statement has to do with observations you made of what was going on in Pristina over the next few days from your home, correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I just want to sigh for the record that this is an area that is very difficult for cross-examination since we -- I have not been able to visit Pristina and so it's very difficult for me to question her about that because I don't know whether she could have seen the things she claims to have seen or not. Had I been there I would know. But I'm told and all I can do is deal with the things I've been told and so my cross-examination will be based on what I think might be the case there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this place that you marked on the map, that you -- where your house was, where you claim to have made all these observations across the city, isn't it the case that there are all kinds of very tall buildings which would have obstructed your view, the opstina, there is a warehouse, there is a bank, there is the Hotel Grand, there is the Kumunda Korpusa [phoen], there is Radio Pristina, there is all kinds of large buildings standing between you and some of the things you claim to have seen, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: The house where I live is in the old part of town, close to the market. At this location, there are no such buildings, no banks, no 15 or 20 storey buildings. It's a part that is in a valley and you can see Vranjevc, Dragodan, Kolovic, and Taslixhe. So all these areas, Dragodan, Kolovic, Taslixhe, are -- the houses in these areas are on the hills so you can see very clearly. And it was not only me that could see the movement of the police forces in Pristina. There were other people who saw the events. My house is not in the centre of Pristina. It is in the centre of Pristina that you find those buildings that you mention, the warehouse, the bank, Radio Pristina and so on. My statement does not say that I saw these things in Dardanija, Lakrish, and other areas where it is impossible to make observations from my house. So I could see Dragodan, I could see the whole of Vranjevc because it's on the side of the hill. I could see Kolovica, which is in the eastern part, to the east of the house where I lived. And Taslixhe which is opposite the house where I live. So these are all hills around the place where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were making observations both during the day and at night, correct?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Both during the day and the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... observations you were making at night, you say you were making with night vision binoculars?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where did you come by night vision binoculars? That's kind of a rare thing for somebody to have.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Of course it is not an instrument that you can find easily. When the OSCE staff left Kosova, they only were allowed 20 kilograms of personal belongings. These binoculars remained in my car. When I drove some of the OSCE mission members to the regional centre in Pristina, which was in the building of Kosova Film.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what make these night vision binoculars were, who made them?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: No, no. That was the first time I used binoculars with that night vision equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell us what you could see through them. What did it look like when you looked through them?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: With those binoculars, at night-time, when there was no electricity and we could hear detonations, blasts, various gunshots in the areas that I mentioned, Dragodan, Vranjevc, Kolovica, Taslixhe, so with these binoculars I saw the movements of the police forces, the army, various cars at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What did they look like? Did you see them in full colour? Like it was the light -- did those binoculars like light it up like it's colour? Or what did it look like to you when you looked through those?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: The colours, when I saw with these binoculars, it was some kind of a light which looked more like a green light. But I could see very clearly the tank, the movement of armed persons, the APCs, the jeeps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How far away were these tanks and APCs and jeeps and persons when you were observing them through these night vision binoculars? How far away were they?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: I don't know the aerial distance because I didn't measure it. I only can say that these areas that I mentioned earlier are not far from where I live. They are close to where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is the map still on the screen there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is the map still on the screen in front of you of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you -- can you show me on that map --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know all the rules, Your Honour. I don't know if she can draw on this map because it's the Prosecutor's exhibit, I don't know if I can have her draw on it or not. I can, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Show me on the map where you were observing these tanks and armoured personnel vehicles and troops and so forth, the movement of them. Show me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think what we need, Mr. Ackerman, is another copy of this map now because this one has already been marked and assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I was wondering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we need to go back to P13 unmarked. Can we have that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Also, Your Honours I would maybe ask that it's been -- zoomed out a little bit so the witness has a better overview of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but -- is that how you want it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want her to first mark on the map her home. Do that again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier I could see this part here. This is the part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you a question now. I just asked you to mark where your house is and you've done that. The next thing I want you to show me is the areas that you were able to observe, things that you thought were important, only by looking through these night vision binoculars. Just make some Xs of the places that you observed, and when you make the X, tell us what you observed there.

utterances.speaker: NAZLIE BALA
utterances.text: Could you put it a little higher, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder whether a snapshot should be taken at this point before it's moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think the map can be moved up a little bit without disturbing what's already happened, can't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When it's moved, Mr. Ackerman, the mark will disappear and you'll need to start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's do a snapshot then and make it an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you sure? Well, it's a pretty pointless one, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is a pointless one. Okay, let's move it up so that she says that she can see all the areas she wants to mark and then we'll do it all over again. I'm sorry, Your Honour, there is no way we are going to finish today now. Not even close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, Ms. Bala is that good enough now or should it be moved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's okay now. I will try to mark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
